articles.text: At a scheduled Piedmont City Council meeting on Monday, December 7, what was expected to be a purely ceremonial meeting thanking outgoing Mayor Bob McBain for his service to the city became quite unexpectedly – and suddenly – a protracted discussion over changing a longstanding unwritten agreement on who serves as vice mayor. Councilmembers initially approved former Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King as the city’s new mayor for two years but devolved into a heated discussion of the process used to select a vice mayor. Council members ultimately voted to have Tim Rood, now entering his sixth year on council, as vice mayor for the current year (2020-21), and council member Jen Cavanaugh as vice mayor for the following year, 2021-22. In Piedmont, the positions of mayor and vice mayor are chosen among city councilmembers. According to city code, “following each general municipal election, the City Council shall elect from among its member officers of the City who shall have the titles of Mayor and Vice-Mayor, each of whom shall serve at the pleasure of the Council.” King was chosen to be the mayor of Piedmont for the next two years, without objection. articles.text: Editor: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) leadership has made continued pleas to not suspend donations during the pandemic. Emily Harrold, a PEF board member, penned a thorough letter last week in the Post, but it was hollow on many points. We all agree that “Paying It Forward” is a notable concept. Supporting our schools is our #1 priority. However we paid it forward in the past, and now we are sorely disappointed in how the Piedmont Unified administration has been navigating through the pandemic – or should we call it fumbling through the pandemic? The only choice for many of us at this time is to suspend PEF donations until we see the PEF itself state it truly – that above all else it wants schools re-opened, even if such opening goes against the hard-to-reach requirements of the administration and teachers’ union. articles.text: Editor: After spending nearly nine years on City Council and three years as mayor, we would like to congratulate and thank Bob McBain for his tireless and inspiring service to our beloved city. Piedmont community members are fortunate to have benefitted from Bob’s commitment and his leadership in many civic roles for nearly two decades. As a member of the Park Commission, it has been my pleasure to work with Bob over the last several years. As the Commission’s liaison, he was attentive to every issue we tackled, offering reasonable, thoughtful guidance and wisdom. Whether our meetings were 45 or 145 minutes, Bob was with us at every moment of every meeting. Bob is one-in-a-million as mayor and man: kind, patient, and loyal. He is generous with tolerance, skimpy with judgement, and brimming with good will for all. From behind the glass door of a shuttered Illy café on Battery Street, the Italian manager waved at me, his hand in a blue disposable glove, with an apologetic smile. For days, his parents, quarantined in Florence over the coronavirus epidemic, had been imploring him to stay away from people. It seemed as if they got their wish granted. Boarding a bus in the strangely empty Salesforce Transbay Terminal, a couple of hand-sanitizers as a parting gift from my colleagues at the bank where I work – or worked? – as a contract writer, I took the first row of seats, to the right of the driver. I didn’t know when I’d be riding home from work again, and I wanted to get an unobstructed view of San Francisco Bay, obliviously magnificent on this spring day. The bridge traffic was light. It took us less than ten minutes to get down to the lower span, from where I could see the white Grand Princess cruise ship docked at an Oakland pier, a lonely helicopter hovering above it. “Princess death,” the driver muttered as we pulled off the bridge and began weaving our way toward the Oakland maze. My neighbor’s parents had been on that ship; they were now at Travis Air Force Base, awaiting the results of their testing. I spent the weekend oscillating between “this can’t be real” and asking myself myriad odd questions, such as whether to explain to the kids, at least to the sixteenyear-old, how to claim our life insurance. I raided the rapidly depleting grocery aisles, picking up things I never thought I’d need, like pinto beans or soap in a 12-pack, all the while feeling the futility of the effort.

Editor: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) leadership has made continued pleas to not suspend donations during the pandemic. Emily Harrold, a PEF board member, penned a thorough letter last week in the Post, but it was hollow on many points. “Fumbling through the pandemic. We paid it forward and were burned.” We all agree that “Paying It Forward” is a notable concept. Supporting our schools is our #1 priority. However we paid it forward in the past, and now we are sorely disappointed in how the Piedmont Unified administration has been navigating through the pandemic – or should we call it fumbling through the pandemic? We “paid it forward” but we were burned. The only choice for many of us at this time is to suspend PEF donations until we see the PEF itself state it truly – that above all else it wants schools re-opened, even if such opening goes against the hard-to-reach requirements of the administration and teachers’ union. Is PEF willing to redirect or withhold some of its donations to the school district to positively impact a re-opening? The Foundation has this power and should exercise it. If PEF is more aligned with the teachers’ union and feels less adamant about re-opening schools, then say it. Put conditions on the next wave of fundng. The bottom line is that student health is suffering. If you, PEF, want to pay it forward for the sake of the kids, demand that schools be re-opened. Emily Harrold asks us to separate the distance learning debate and our willingness to donate to PEF. This is not a reasonable request. Who donates to an organization if they disagree with its stance – a murky one in this case. Sorry, PEF. articles.text: Nominations are currently being accepted for the 28th annual Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame, honoring exceptional women who make a difference in their communities countywide. Honorees will be celebrated in 2021 during an event co-hosted by the Alameda County Board of Supervisors and the Alameda County Commission on the Status of Women. The Women’s Hall of Fame is now accepting nominations in 13 categories: Business and Professions; Community Service; Culture and Art; Education; Emerging Leader; Environment; Health; Justice; Non-Traditional Careers; Philanthropy; Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics; Sports and Athletics; and Youth Services. You can nominate a community leader in any of these categories by visiting http://www.acgov.org/whof/nominations.htm. Nominations will be open year-round. The inductee should be established in her career or volunteerism with significant achievements that have benefited communities in Alameda County, should be successful in overcoming personal and professional obstacles, and is a role model for youth and women who strive to achieve their own success. More than 250 women have been inducted into the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame since its inception in 1993. In addition to honoring exceptional women leaders from Alameda County, the annual event raises funds for youth scholarships and supports local nonprofit community partners serving women, youth and families. “As we honor the remarkable 13 inductees, we also celebrate the 100th anniversary of the 19th Amendment [of the U.S. Constitution], guaranteeing and protecting women’s constitutional right to vote,” stated County Administrator Susan S. Muranishi. “In the past 100 years we have seen women become mayors, governors, Congresswomen, and now elected as Vice President of the United States of America. We commend the trailblazing women who came before us and make way for female pioneers to lead us through the next 100 years.” You can watch this year’s Hall of Fame ceremony and learn more about the honorees at: https:// www.classy.org/campaign/2020- alameda-county-womens-hall-offame/c298882. The date for the 2021 event will be determined after inductees are chosen early next year. articles.text: Editor: On behalf of Berkeley Symphony, I am submitting this letter in support of a Bay Area jewel, The Piedmont Center for the Arts. articles.text: I am writing to express my thanks to Former Mayor Bob McBain. The computer gods intervened to prevent the City Clerk from seeing my virtual raised hand at the Council Meeting on Monday night. I did want to praise Bob in person following his remarks culminating his tenure on the City Council. Bob made reference to his 30 years of residence; my time as a resident is more than twice that. During that period, I have seen at least 30 mayors finish their terms of office. One thing they all have in common is their peaceful surrender of office to their duly elected successors. Bob followed that tradition as well. In other respects, Mayor McBain’s tenure was unique. I don’t think any prior mayor has had such difficult circumstances with which to cope. And yet his performance has been outstanding. I truly regret we have term limits in our Charter, as I would love for Bob’s calm, competent and dedicated style of leadership to see us Piedmonters through to the conclusion of the pandemic. Bob took office at a time of financial and political turmoil in Piedmont. We had even made the national news in a most unfavorable light. Bob took the helm, and things began to improve. In surprisingly short time Bob ushered in an era of good will, financial stability and happy times. Had the pandemic not intervened, I believe the good times would have continued to the present. For evidence of Piedmonters’ contentment I cite the overwhelming support given the renewal of the City’s Parcel Tax. Critical appointments overseen by Bob will influence things in Piedmont for years to come. The appointment of Sara Lillevand to be City Administrator has shown huge dividends already as she copes with the pandemic and her duty to keep us all as safe as possible. Equally important was the appointment of Betsy Andersen to the City Council. Without Betsy and Bob’s leadership, we would not have passed a bond measure to build a community swimming complex. For years the pool issue has vexed one City Council after another. Now we have a first-class solution! The real need for leadership of a completely unscripted nature struck in March with the arrival of Covid 19. While Bob was already a constant fixture around City Hall, the demands on the shoulders of Bob, Sara and their team have been enormous – and have they ever risen to the task. Bob has laid a foundation for the new Council to follow, and he wished them well Monday night. Had Bob’s farewell taken place in the Council Chamber I would have called for all to give him a standing ovation. Bob McBain has been a Mayor for the Ages!
articles.title: In praise of Bob McBain – a mayor for the ages

articles.text: Total cases in Piedmont rise to 71 Alameda County is currently undergoing the most severe of COVID-19 cases since the pandemic began. Officials issued a new stay-at-home order for the entire county, which includes Piedmont, that began Monday, December 7. On Friday, December 4, a total of 668 new cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Alameda County, the highest number of cases in a single day. The worst day for the pandemic in Alameda County prior to this was August 13, when 417 cases were recorded. There have been several days in the past two weeks with far more new cases than the surge in August, when daily new cases were previously at their highest levels. Six new cases of COVID-19 were reported among Piedmonters since last week, bringing the city’s total to 71 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. The City has closed playgrounds in accordance with the Alameda County health orders, otherwise, Piedmont’s parks will remain open until further notice. “It is important that our entire community take action to stem the spread of this disease by limiting interactions with people outside their household,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said in a statement this week. “Our collective well-being is at stake and we owe it to each other to keep our community safe.” The new stay-at-home order is aimed at limiting in-person interactions between people from different households. Restaurants must reduce operations to take-out and delivery only, and outdoor and indoor dining are now prohibited. Museums, movie theatres, zoos and personal care businesses, like hair salons, must close. Outdoor children’s playgrounds are also now shuttered. Among the local venues to close temporarily are Oakland Zoo, Children’s Fairyland and Chabot Space & Science Center. Malls, shopping centers and retail stores can remain open with capacity restrictions. The county health order is connected to a supplemental state health order that went into effect this month due to coronavirus cases spiking across California. The state order is activated when a regional group of counties, such as the Bay Area, announces that ICU capacity has dropped below 15 percent. While the Bay Area has not reached that threshold, health authorities from five Bay Area counties agreed to adopt the stricter stay-at-home restrictions as a precaution. “Rising hospitalization rates across the region threaten not only our community members with severe COVID-19, but anyone who may need care because of a heart attack, stroke, accident or other critical health need,” Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss said in a statement last week. “By acting together now we will have the greatest impact on the surge and save more lives.” The health orders in the Bay Area are scheduled to remain in place until January 4 but could be extended. Overall in Alameda County, the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 5.9 percent, a metric that has swelled upward since the start of November. The total case load in the county is now 33,736, an increase of over 3,800 cases from one week ago, according to the Alameda County Department of Public Health yesterday, Tuesday, December 8. Tragically, 11 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 525. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 11,833. In Hayward, 5,145 cases have been recorded and there have been 2,670 reported in Fremont. San Leandro reported 1,929, Livermore reported 1,584, Union City reported 1,390 and Berkeley reported 1,328. The rising case rate caused the state last month to put the entire county into the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system for reopening businesses and activities. As of yesterday, Tuesday, December 8, the county’s case rate is 15.7 cases per 100,000 people, a massive increase from one week ago. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. Only four of 58 Californian counties are not in the Purple Tier. The state and county are urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes an alarming flood of cases throughout the United States even as several COVID-19 vaccine options appear to be on the horizon. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 1,389,707 cases of COVID-19 in California. Cases have trended upward since October 18. A total of 20,047 deaths have been recorded statewide.
articles.title: COVID-19 cases reaching all-time highs in Alameda County

articles.text: Police Officer Willie Wright was promoted to the rank of Sergeant on December 5 after 10 years with the City. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers appointed him to position in advance of the retirement later this month of Sgt. Nicole Bolden. As a Watch Commander Wright will be in charge of a group of officers in addition to a records clerk, dispatcher and animal control officer. He will continue to function as the department’s defensive tactics instructor and taser instructor. Prior to his promotion Wright served as a Patrol Officer, Field Training Officer and also was a Detective for four years. The topic, “California’s New Normal: Drought and Deluge,” focused on “California’s pressing water issues,” Trainor explained. “For the past 23 years, Ashley has led the organization in bringing together industry, scientists, and environmental leaders in government, groups that often have divergent views. It was California’s first “water law” in over a century. “[The act] is probably California’s most important climate adaptation strategy, and we must continue to implement that law,” Boren said. The worst day for the pandemic in Alameda County prior to this was August 13, when 417 cases were recorded. There have been several days in the past two weeks with far more new cases than the surge in August, when daily new cases were previously at their highest levels. Six new cases of COVID-19 were reported among Piedmonters since last week, bringing the city’s total to 71 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. The City has closed playgrounds in accordance with the Alameda County health orders, otherwise, Piedmont’s parks will remain open until further notice. “It is important that our entire community take action to stem the spread of this disease by limiting interactions with people outside their household,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said in a statement this week. “Our collective well-being is at stake and we owe it to each other to keep our community safe.” The new stay-at-home order is aimed at limiting in-person interactions between people from different households. Restaurants must reduce operations to take-out and delivery only, and outdoor and indoor dining are now prohibited. Museums, movie theatres, zoos and personal care businesses, like hair salons, must close. Outdoor children’s playgrounds are also now shuttered. Among the local venues to close temporarily are Oakland Zoo, Children’s Fairyland and Chabot Space & Science Center. Malls, shopping centers and retail stores can remain open with capacity restrictions. The county health order is connected to a supplemental state health order that went into effect this month due to coronavirus cases spiking across California. The state order is activated when a regional group of counties, such as the Bay Area, announces that ICU capacity has dropped below 15 percent. While the Bay Area has not reached that threshold, health authorities from five Bay Area counties agreed to adopt the stricter stay-at-home restrictions as a precaution. “Rising hospitalization rates across the region threaten not only our community members with severe COVID-19, but anyone who may need care because of a heart attack, stroke, accident or other critical health need,” Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss said in a statement last week. “By acting together now we will have the greatest impact on the surge and save more lives.” The health orders in the Bay Area are scheduled to remain in place until January 4 but could be extended. Overall in Alameda County, the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 5.9 percent, a metric that has swelled upward since the start of November. The total case load in the county is now 33,736, an increase of over 3,800 cases from one week ago, according to the Alameda County Department of Public Health yesterday, Tuesday, December 8. Tragically, 11 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 525. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 11,833. In Hayward, 5,145 cases have been recorded and there have been 2,670 reported in Fremont. San Leandro reported 1,929, Livermore reported 1,584, Union City reported 1,390 and Berkeley reported 1,328. The rising case rate caused the state last month to put the entire county into the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system for reopening businesses and activities. As of yesterday, Tuesday, December 8, the county’s case rate is 15.7 cases per 100,000 people, a massive increase from one week ago. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. Only four of 58 Californian counties are not in the Purple Tier. The state and county are urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes an alarming flood of cases throughout the United States even as several COVID-19 vaccine options appear to be on the horizon. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 1,389,707 cases of COVID-19 in California. Cases have trended upward since October 18. A total of 20,047 deaths have been recorded statewide. articles.text: What better way to celebrate the end of 2020 than with a Virtual Instrumental Music Concert featuring the Piedmont Middle and High School Band and Orchestra Classes! The PMS/ PHS Virtual Winter Concert will be streamed from youtube on Wednesday, December 16 at 7 pm. A link to the event will be emailed to families prior to Wednesday, Dec 16th. The Virtual Concert will feature pieces by each of the following performing groups; the PMS Advanced Orchestra, 7th grade Band, 8th grade Band, PHS Orchestra, PHS Symphonic Band, PHS Jazz Band and PHS Jazz Combo. Small ensembles, as well as a selected number of solo and duets are also on the program. Band pieces on the program include Seasons of Love from the musical Rent, Arabian Nights from the Disney movie Aladdin, What a Wonderful World, made famous by Louis Armstrong, and the Liberty Bell March by John Phillip Sousa, among others. The acclaimed PHS Jazz Combo, given the highest rating awarded at the CMEA Bay Section Jazz Combo Festival in February 2020, will also perform. This quintet of advanced PHS Jazz students who practice weekly in an outdoor socially distanced setting, include seniors Liam Charron on keyboard, and Connor Stratman on alto saxophone; as well as juniors Will Davies on drums, Jason Machle on guitar, and Alex Tafapolsky on bass. Band teacher Andria Mullan and orchestra teacher Jessica Ivry have put in many hours of audio and photo editing to make this concert happen. Mullan especially thanks PHS band seniors Jackson Nooney and Liam Charron, who produced the high school Symphonic, Pep Band and Jazz Band audio tracks, and Thomas Yu and Connor Stratman, who produced the high school Band video tracks. A link to the concert will be emailed to all Band and Orchestra families prior to December 16. All families in Piedmont School District will also receive an email with the link. Early each autumn, Cori and Zach Kau, parents of two children at Havens and one at PMS, make a generous contribution to the Giving Campaign. “We support the Giving Campaign every year, because it builds our community and ensures that our schools and children have the resources to excel. Piedmont has been a very special place to raise our children that is rooted in a sense of community and scholastic values,” said Cori. They immediately submit their gift receipt to Zach’s company so that the Giving Campaign can also benefit from a company match. Who doesn’t like free money? Piedmont Education Foundation is encouraging supporters to apply for a company match once they have made their donation. Many of the largest Bay Area companies, including Apple, Wells Fargo, PG&E, Disney/ Pixar, Google, and more have matching gift programs for their employees. Each company has its own system for processing matching gifts, but generally all that is needed is a donation tax receipt, which Giving Campaign donors receive by email. It’s not only big companies that do matching programs. PEF Executive Director Heather Frank encourages donors to ask their organizations about gift matching. “Many companies recognize what a benefit it is to match their employee contributions. Not only does it help with employee morale, the company receives tax benefits and additional, positive marketing from nonprofit recipients,” she said. Frank said that in prior years multiple donors have requested and received matches from companies including Apple, BlackRock, BNY Mellon, Charles Schwab, Chevron, Clif Bar, Disney, Genentech, Google, Lawrence Livermore, PG&E, Salesforce, Visa, and Wells Fargo. These matches, Frank adds, are not insignificant. “Last year, the PEF Giving Campaign received matching gifts from 71 different companies, totaling $327,000.” In January, PEF will publish the names of the donors for this year’s Giving Campaign. If you have not yet made a contribution, please visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/donate, and remember to ask your company about their matching gift program.

articles.text: The Piedmont Makers successfully raised over $420,000 for the Engineering Lab in Piedmont High School’s new STEAM building. The funds will be used for computer-aided fabrication equipment such as a CNC router, laser cutter, 3D printers and more. It will also employ a dedicated lab staff member to help teachers shape course offerings. The school board will consider approval of the Engineering Lab gift at its meeting on December 15. Since the Engineering Lab was first discussed with the School Board in July, Makers has engaged with the school administration, teachers, and community to continue to shape the proposal. With a state-of-the-art engineering lab, teachers will work with the lab manager to take advantage of the new equipment to adapt current courses that teach Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) including engineering, as well as creating new courses. The engineering lab will be a workshop for design and prototyping, equipped with both manual and computer-controlled tools. It is a modern version of a wood or metal workshop and should allow PHS students to make almost anything: big or small; technical or artistic; serious or whimsical. The Piedmont Makers group was founded in 2014 to support and inspire S.T.E.A.M. education in Piedmont at all grade levels. Programs include events like the annual School Maker Faire and robotics. In the last four years, the Piedmont Makers robotics programs have grown from one team with 10 high school students to 34 teams and 220 students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The donation of $420,000 marks the largest capital campaign in the history of Piedmont Makers. Makers has also continued to support the district through other donations such as over 30 LEGO Mindstorms kits donated to Piedmont Middle School this fall and $10k in teacher grants that will be disbursed in early 2021. When the engineering lab is completed, the lab will function as the home base for the Piedmont Highlanders FRC (FIRST Robotics Competition) Team. FIRST Robotics Competition is the highest level of FIRST Robotics. The team will operate as a Piedmont High School team with a faculty advisor. The Engineering Lab is on the first floor of the STEAM building facing the interior of campus.

articles.text: Paris, the City of Lights, is magical at Christmas, but while different, this year has many similar traditions. The lights turned up last week inside department stores and neighborhood shops. The store openings were widely heralded after Parisians endured the entire month of November on lockdown. Retailers were chomping at the bit for Christmastime buying to begin as they try to climb out of the disastrous sales in 2020. Street trees and store windows are dressed up in their best holiday goldware, twinkling seductively for shoppers to hurry in. The temperature is chilly with misty showers and sidewalks full of people and shopping bags, so it feels just like a normal Christmas. Starting December 4th Black Friday sales were everywhere, with featured goods up to 50% off as a way to bring in the hordes. We’re not sure people know what Black Friday is, but the concept, not unlike the United States, starts after Thanksgiving when merchants start to hope that the winding-down selling days for the year begin to move from red ink deficient to black ink and create prosperity. A Parisian symbol of the City of Lights and an oasis for shopping is Galleries Lafayette, which occupies the entire block of Boulevard Haussmann on the Right Bank. After a metro ride we exited at Rue de la Chaussée D’Antin, where we climbed out of the cavernous underground to the reveal of flashing, vividly hued window displays. Galleries was a luxury bazaar by design, and this is the 1912 Flagship store. It’s on everybody’s must-see list for its spectacular steel and glass dome, a department store inspired for the theater world and Paris Opera. The founders pioneered production of store-brand merchandise: high-fashion styles that were well-made and sold at budget prices. Still very much their marketing edge, this successful enterprise has expanded to 62 Galleries Lafayette locations worldwide. Each Christmas the largest tree imaginable is suspended from the dome. articles.text: Staff Photo Piedmont’s cross-country team has qualified for State Met for seven years, but the event was canceled this year due to COVID. Last week, the California Interscholastic Federation announced that it was canceling its both its Sectional and State championship meets. It also pushed official team workouts into January in response to a spike in COVID-19 spike throughout the state. The CIF decision to cancel North Coast Section playoffs affects all teams, but the termination of the state championship impacts only one program – cross country, Piedmont’s girls’ team has qualified for the State Championship in Woodward Park for seven years. At this time last year Sophia Zalewski just put the finishing touch of her high school career at the State Meet placing 11th in a crowded field of 212 runners. But this year, with COVID-19, a field of that magnitude was unrealistic to run, and the CIF canceled it entirely. “Given what is going around in the country and world, it makes sense for us not to have State this year. With all the people it takes to put on the state championship, it is completely understandable,” said PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund. The CIF decision mentioned that the cancelation of postseason competition gives an added opportunity for leagues like the Western Alameda County Conference to schedule more meets. “The state can change anything they put out, so the CIF and NCS don’t really give us announcements quickly. We wait for an official notice, then it gets pushed, then we wait again,” said Holmlund. For the WACC and its 12 member schools with cross country programs, there is some optimism that teams can schedule some sort of competition. Holmlund said that league officials are Staff Photo discussing possible options, but no plans have been announced. “What’s happening is our league is discussing possible options of what we could do to provide some kind of competition for our athletes in whatever sport, the WACC may develop an alternative plan to what the CIF and NCS lays out. We’re hopeful we’ll have one or two local competitions,” mentioned Holmlund. There has been some discussion about pushing Season 1 sports into the spring, which would merge Cross Country with Track and Field. Currently the CIF defines Season 1 sports as: football, water polo, girls’ volleyball, and cross country. The solace for Piedmont and its student-athletes is that their plans for working out in pods gained support from the school district. Kids are still eligible for some sporting structure in this uncertain time. “We’re still in the summer-conditioning realm until we become a season. Until we get official word, everything is conditioning and cross country is starting [Monday]. We’re working in Pictured is Adri McAuliffe (1256) at the State Meet a year ago. pods without equipment. We’ve been doing a lot of hill-work, now we have access to the track and we’ll be starting longer mileage workouts,” said Holmlund. “The school determined that the kids getting out to run and exercise was important for their mental health,” added the coach. Until this point, the cross country program was operating off-campus through the city’s Recreation Department, not the school district. That alone raises significant questions about the level of support being provided by PUSD and the high school. In the meantime colleges are eager to know how high school students are self-motivating without official sport activities. “This time takes a lot of mental toughness. We have some students who have really gotten into their running on their own. We definitely have those kids who have been persistent about getting out the door and running,” said Holmlund. Three months after the start of the school year, the cross country team will gain a bit more structure now that Witter Field is available to them. More information should be available on Season 1 sports on January 1, or in the days shortly afterward. It was a terrific Saturday, December 5 for the University of California and Stanford football programs. The Golden Bears pulled off a dramatic 21-17 upset over the No. 21 Oregon Ducks, and the Cardinal were equally as magical with a 31-26 defeat of the No. 23 Washington Huskies. The Bears’ unexpected victory over Oregon provided its first win of the season and keeps California in possible bowl contention. To qualify for a bowl game, Cal has to finish with a .500 record. They face the 1-2 Washington State Cougars this Saturday, December 12. The Cougars defeated Oregon State 38-28. The Bears will have one remaining regular season game on December 19 against a team that has yet to be determined. Cal enters as the early favorites against the Cougars, which use a run-and-shoot heavily pass oriented offense that will try to tire out the Bears’ defense. It’s a similar scheme to the “Air Raid” offense that Berkeley ran under Sonny Dykes. It spells well for Cal’s talented defensive backfield, but they must stay consistent. Bears’ coach Justin Wilcox said they are preparing for a cold-weather fight on the gridiron. “Guys that handle the ball, keeping their hands warm ... there’s different ways to do that and we’ll have all that ready for them. Whether it’s 23 or 33 [degrees], clear or snowing or somewhere in between, it’s another chance for us to play in a great environment. articles.text: Photo courtesy of ArizonaSports.com Arizona State guard Remy Martin has the Sun Devils ranked No. 23 in the NCAA. Oregon is expected to have a top-25 ranking. Two weeks into the 2020-21 NCAA men’s basketball season, let’s loo at Pac-12 schools. The No. 23 Sun Devils of Arizona State are the only team in the conference currently in the top 25, holding a 3-1 overall record and 1-0 in the league after defeating Cal 70-62 on December 3. They have a team boasting returning starter G Remy Martin, who seems to be the leading candidate for the Conference Player of the Year honors. Marvin Bagley and Josh Christopher seem to be future NBA talents as well. Tomorrow, ASU plays its biggest game of the year against No. 24 San Diego State. Oregon received 26 votes to receive ranking in the top 25, currently at 2-1 with a season-opening 83-75 loss to Missouri. Currently just outside a ranking, wins against Florida A&M today, Washington on Saturday, and UCLA on Dec. 23 could be catapult their ranking. Washington State received three top-25 votes, and is 3-0 with three narrow victories to start their schedule. They will have winnable contests until facing ASU on December 31 to end 2020. Guard Isaac Bonton is their leading player. The UCLA Bruins were the preseason No. 1 by Pac-12 media polls; currently 3-1 as well, but lost to the SDSU Aztecs 73-58 to open the season on Nov. 25. The Arizona Wildcats, a usual NCAA basketball powerhouse, are 3-0 without their top six scorers from last season. But they bring back the nation’s No. 5 ranked recruiting class from last year. Arizona’s first test will be Stanford on December 19. The Cardinal is 2-2 after a healthy slate of early games, including a 4-point loss (67-63) to No. 16 North Carolina on Dec. 1. Senior forward Oscar da Silva leads a healthy returning cast, meaning Stanford will challenge the top teams in the conference despite not currently having a ranking. They face USC on Sunday, December 13 and Arizona the following Saturday. Over to the Trojans of Southern California, they are 4-1 and freshman forward Evan Mobley could be the newcomer of the year for the Pac-12. His brother, Isaiah Mobley, a fellow McDonalds All-American, make a tough combination to deal with. The Trojans play Stanford in their next contest, but also play the difficult San Francisco Dons, which are 4-2 and upset No. 18 Virginia 61-60 on Nov. 27. The Golden Bears of Berkeley will largely play upsetters this year. With a 2-3 overall record, the Bears gave the Sun Devils some fight in their 70-62 loss on Dec. 3, but will require large contributions out of an unproven roster, which includes former WACC star Monty Bowser from O’Dowd. articles.text: The Las Vegas Raiders walked out of Week 13 with its heads held high after Derek Carr pulled off late-game heroics with a touchdown heave to Henry Ruggs, beating the Jets 31-28. The Raiders got it done, but was not impressive against a winless New York Jets squad that is poised to get the No. 1 overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. Now improving its record to 7-5, Vegas is still in the AFC playoff hunt but still on the outside looking in and one game behind the Indianapolis Colts and Miami Dolphins, both teams on their remaining schedule. But the Raiders can control their destiny this week against the Colts, a difficult matchup with veteran quarterback Philip Rivers and a stout defense. Although Vegas has proven to show up for critical games, upsetting Indy will be tough. A defensive game will likely lean toward a Colts’ win, while Carr, head coach Jon Gruden, and Co. will have to force a high scoring game. Going with my gut, the Colts should win a one-possession ballgame. SF 49ers As for the 49ers, they took a predictable defeat to the Bills but are still in the NFC Wild Card hunt one game back of Vikings. Now scheduled to play this weekend in Arizona due to COVID complications, they will host Washington, a game that will reunite veteran quarterback Alex Smith with the franchise which drafted him back in 2005 out of Utah. Smith, hands down the NFL Comeback Player of the Year, famously recovered from life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis due to complications from leg surgery. Both teams are 5-7, while Washington is tied for the NFC East lead with its solid defense under recently hired head coach Ron Rivera, an All-American when playing for Cal. This is a more difficult game to predict, and SF would certainly be the hands-down favorite with a healthy roster. The 49ers’ offense will have the tools available to beat Washington with running back Raheem Mostert, and receivers Deebo Samuel, and Brandon Aiyuk. But they’ll have to use quick plays to avoid Washington’s Photo courtesy of Las Vegas Review-Journal Raiders’ rookie receiver Henry Ruggs scored the game-winner in Vegas’ 31-28 win over the Jets. The 49ers are favored against Washington, the home of former San Francisco QB Alex Smith. strong pass rush. It is hard to bet against Washington after it handed the Steelers their first loss of the season. Should the 49ers’ pass defense prove more useful early on, SF could win. If Washington is able to disrupt 49ers QB Nick Mullens, it could be a big day for the East Coast team. Golden State to start season The Warriors are back with Stephen Curry, Draymond Green, but not Klay Thompson due a second consecutive devastating season-ending injury. Their preseason starts this Saturday, December 12 against the Denver Nuggets. They move into 2021 with Curry, Green, first-round pick James Wiseman at center, Andrew Wiggins, and recently acquired forward Kelly Oubre. It’s hard to see the Warriors pulling off the same look as in recent years, where its triangle offense kept teams dizzy from its shooting options. Without Thompson, the Warriors’ offense could become pick-and-roll centric with Curry running the floor. With Wiseman, Green, Oubre, and Kevon Looney, Golden State has a large squad capable of being physical with any team in the league, which will be critical when facing defending champion LA Lakers. The Spurs’ shutout Arsenal 2-0 in last week’s match of the week, the North London Derby. After losing 3-2 to Germany’s RB Leipzig, they were relegated to Europa League. In previous issues we’ve discussed United giving Solskjær the boot, and the “Ole Out” campaign continues in full force. But will it happen? Its loss to Leipzig seemed like the perfect storm. Superstar midfielder Paul Pogba’s agent dropped a bomb in a recent interview saying that his client was on the way out of Manchester. With January 1 as the opening date of the transfer window, it could be now or never for Manchester United and likelihood of making a move shrinking by the day. articles.text: • • Califor nia State Parks announced on Friday, December 4, that campgrounds will be temporarily closed for regions within the Purple Tier of the state’s stay-at-home orders. Day use for parks will still be permitted. That includes all of Alameda County. “Yesterday, California took an important step to address the alarming pace of COVID-19 case rates that are threatening to overwhelm the health care delivery system,” said California State Parks Director Armando Quintero. “While the new Regional Stay at Home Order is asking Californians to stay home as much as possible and for campground sites in impacted regions to close, the state also recognizes that that outdoor activity is critical for mental health and physical health. We welcome you to recreate in the outdoors provided that you stay local, plan ahead to find out what is open, wear a face covering, practice physical distancing and avoid gatherings with people outside the immediate household. The California State Park systems issued several guidelines in response to the COVID-19 spike throughout the state, asking its day-use patrons to consider the following: • Stay Local – Stay close to home to slow the spread of COVID-19. Do not travel if you or someone in your household is sick. • Plan Ahead – Prior to leaving home, check the webpage of the park unit you plan to visit to find out if it is open, if parking is available, and what visitor guidelines are in effect. • Stay Safer at 6-feet – Maintain a physical distance of six feet or more. Visitors are being asked to leave if there are too many people to allow for the required physical distance. • Boating – Do not raft up to other boaters or pull up onto a beach next to other patrons. Keep Clean – Not all restrooms are open to the public. Bring soap/hand sanitizer. Please pack out all trash. Stay Covered – Individuals must have a face covering with them at all times. The state’s Regional Stay at Home Order has been implemented for areas with less than 15 percent of existing capacity in ICU units in hospitals. This includes, Northern California, Bay Area, Greater Sacramento, San Joaquin Valley and Southern California. State campground sites within these regions will be temporarily closed in accordance with the new order. Yosemite also limited to day-use Yosemite National Park also announced that they are have limited accress for day-use only starting December 7 in response to the Regional Stay at Home orders. The park will be closed from 5 p.m. to 8 a.m. “Hotels and campgrounds are closed. Wilderness permits are not available. While the wilderness (including big wall climbing) is open, overnight stays in wilderness (including on big walls) is prohibited… All visitors must leave the park by 5 p.m.,” a notice from the park stated. Yosemite added that it will continue working with Mariposa County to determine a timeline for a full park reopening. “Yosemite National Park is working closely with officials from Mariposa County Public Health and the California Department of Public Health to implement California’s regional Stay Home order. Consistent with the Governor’s order, these temporary restrictions will remain in effect until local conditions change,” it stated. articles.text: Area reopened November 21 after wildfire closure Sunol Regional Wilderness of East Bay Regional Park District was reopened on November 21 after recovering from the SCU complex fires that raged for 44 days this fire season. Sunol Regional Wilderness is now open, so you can explore and enjoy all of the trails within the park boundary. The adjacent Ohlone Wilderness remains closed, however. The area is among the smaller of parks operated by East Bay Regional, but it is one of the more popular destinations due to Little Yosemite – a frequented water hole in the warmer months. The lack of rain this winter has reduced the creek to a trickle that feeds into the more active Alameda Creek area. Right now the trail is more of a beginners’ course in canyoning as you climb over boulders; keeping sharp eyes on where to put your feet, hands for secure landing spots. The walk from the Sunol Regional parking lot is a mellow 1.1 miles from the gate on Ohlone Road. Adjacent to the main trail is a more secluded path along the creek, eventually re-emerging with Ohlone Road on the way to Little Yosemite. The path down to the Little Yosemite area is narrow, and depending on the time of the day and year, you will likely be taking your time – especially during a time of COVID. Little Yosemite is a popular swimming hole, where giant boulders provide a beginner’s course in rock climbing and canyoning.

Adjacent to the main trail is a more secluded path along the creek, eventually re-emerging with Ohlone Road on the way to Little Yosemite. During the warmer months, and with more water, the area is popular for hikers and swimmers. Photos by Jonathan Comeaux Alameda Creek runs along the Ohlone Road trail on the way to Sunol Regional Park’s Little Yosemite. Midway to ur destination, I had already passed 36 people, which would have undoubtedly doubled had we stayed on the main pathway for the entire walk. Don’t fret if you are COVID-conscious; the foot traffic thin out from there on. Another 1.1 miles away is the McCorkle trail, where we only passed four people, and then another four people on the remaining four miles miles on the way back to the car – a total of rounding 7 people per mile for the total hike. The four-mile McCorkle Trail was secluded and had only two couples passing by. The McCorkle loop starts your ascent. We topped out at 1,335 feet in elevation gain, but the medium slope means it is not over-challenging. The trails through the hills are shared with grazing cows, which means you may get uncomfortably close to them and be dodging cow-pies for a short distance. Although the cows seem to be accustomed to hikers, dog walkers should take notice. Following the McCorkle Trail back to the entrance gate on Ohlone Road will provide a sweeping view of Sunol Regional’s foothills, cows grazing through the winter-stripped grasslands, and the vibrant color of orange leaves throughout the area. The ascent up provides a glimpse of the Calaveras Reservoir. Punch in “Sunol Regional Wilderness” into your GPS device to access this park. The dry creek bed of Alameda Creek past Little Yosemite. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre presents The Steadfast Tin Solider, written and directed by Mary Zimmerman, a noted playwright, available to stream until December 27. The play was produced by Looking Glass Theatre Company in Chicago. Zimmerman’s extravagant play is inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s story of the same title. The play features the unlikely adventure of a little tin solider that exudes a ton of bravery, and is infused with Zimmerman’s blend of storytelling through image and movement, accompanied by musicians. The Chicago Tribune called it a “treat for all ages. Barely more than an hour long, this major new work is one holiday experience you don’t want to miss.” Looking Glass Theatre Company’s The Steadfast Tin Solider. Tickets are available for one livestream performance plus access to video on demand. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/season/2021/steadfasttinsoldier.asp for purchasing information.

articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company is presenting its first ever drive-in movie theatre event, with five screenings of Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker to be projected on the north wall of the historic Paramount Theatre. Although indoor theaters and performances remain closed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Oakland Ballet Company is continuing its annual tradition of bringing The Nutcracker to audiences from a safe distance. Screenings of the performance will take place Sunday through Thursday, December 20-24, at 6 p.m. each day. The parking lot located at 2100 Telegraph Avenue will open at 4:30 p.m. to ticket holders. This performance will mark the 49th year that the company will present a production of The Nutcracker. With a runtime of approximately 75 minutes, Lustig’s Nutcracker includes excerpts from the ballet’s 2019 producOakland Ballet Company will present The Nutcracker on outside wall of the Paramount Theatre. tion with original choreography. Since his appointment as Artistic Director in 2010, Lustig has revitalized the company, helping the organization reclaim its position as a leading arts institution in the Bay Area. He was trained at the Royal Ballet School in London, and has danced with the Dutch National Ballet and Birmingham Royal Ballet before joining the Oakland group. In addition to the Oakland Ballet Company’s professional ensemble, the production features more than 40 Bay Area dancers, ages 7 to 17, in the roles of snowballs, mice, soldiers and candies, with musical accompaniment from the Oakland Symphony and members of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Visit oaklandballet.org to secure tickets before the event. Tickets are limited. No on-site tickets will be available.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet to show The Nutcracker in drive-in screening at Paramount Dec. 20–24

articles.text: San Francisco Opera has found an intriguing way to bring the “stage” to audiences safely – by showing filmed productions of operas at the newly created drive-in theater at San Francisco’s Fort Mason. This weekend’s production is Tosca, an opera in three acts by Giacomo Puccini, with libretto by Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa, and based on the drama La Tosca by Victorien Sardou. It will run on Friday and Saturday this weekend, December 11 and 12, at 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. both days. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré I am often reminded that people still love to be told a good story. And there is no medium that does this more powerfully than film. A fine example is the recently released The King’s Speech. It is extraordinary. A wonderful surprise. That it was ever made is remarkable. Imagine trying to pitch to a studio this very English film, set in the 1920s and 30s, about a shy man, Albert the Duke of York, albeit the future King of England, who possesses a stammer that has tormented him all of his life. Albert, aka Bertie (Colin Firth), has always been content (resigned, perhaps) to live his life in the shadow of his older brother, Edward (Guy Pearce), who is first in line to the throne held by their father, the overbearing and unsympathetic George V (Michael Gambon). For decades, Bertie has hidden from his family and the public ever fearful that in the midst of a mundane conversation his throat will close off, his words incarcerated by an uncontrollable stammer. The thought of standing before a microphone at a public speaking engagement sends him into a paroxysm of panic and harrowing silence. Wishing to overcome this affliction, he sees speech experts of questionable practices, one filling his mouth with ice cubes while insisting that they can cure him. Another encourages him to smoke, claiming that it relaxes the throat. He is deeply frustrated and constantly humiliated. Finally, his wife, the Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter), desperate, finds Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an eccentric speech therapist, who uses unorthodox methods and patiently explains to both the Duchess and the Duke that if they give him total control and their trust he can help Bertie do that which has eluded him all of his life: speech that is liberated and flows freely. And so begins the essence of the film: the creation of an improbable relationship between two men, Logue, the Australian expatriate and commoner, and the Albert, royalty, whose only wish is that he never have to assume Colin Firth portrayed Albert the Duke of York in The King’s Speech. the crown as the King of England. Their relationship, tentative and combative at first, filled with resistance and distrust, takes on a special importance when Bertie’s brother, Edward, is crowned King Edward VIII after the death of their father, George V. Edward, it turns out, scandalizing all of England, announces that he will abdicate the throne in order to marry Wallis Simpson (Eve Best), an American divorcee. That decision requires that Albert, next in succession, step forward and assume that singular role, the prospect of which has always terrified him. How can he ever speak to the people of England as their king when he can’t speak to his family or to Logue without a debilitating stutter? Adding to the exigencies of his position is the fact that England is on the cusp of war with Germany. Albert, who is soon to become King George VI, must reassure and inspire his countrymen during a period that will be characterized as their finest hour. And he must do this standing before a microphone. The relationship created between Logue and the Duke is touching, filled with humor and tension and scatological rants (Bertie never stammers when he’s angry and cussing). To watch the two men spar, teacher and pupil, is to observe two deeply gifted actors deliver the performances of their lives, while supported by the members of an astonishing ensemble – a dream cast. The King’s Speech is a brilliantly recreated moment in history that otherwise would have likely been just a footnote to those years leading up to World War II. Happily it isn’t. The King’s Speech. Starring Colin Firth, Helena Bonham Carter, Geoffrey Rush, Guy Pearce, Timothy Spall Derek Jacobi, Michael Gambon and Jennifer Ehle. Directed by Tom Hooper. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. articles.text: Helen Mirren and Ian McKellen stars in The Good Liar. Movie review by Chris Honoré The pleasure to be found in The Good Liar resides not in the story, though the first two acts are intriguing . It is in watching Helen Mirren and Ian McKellan, both knighted, portraying two attractive people, Betty and Roy, engaging in the initial drama of, well, not courtship exactly, but friendly companionship. Or so it seems. Initially we meet them seated across a posh restaurant table making introductions, smiling, having a drink. Both widowed, they’ve met online and this is their first opportunity to put a face to their correspondence. She is a retired Oxford professor, apparently affluent, lovely, and smart. He is… well, it’s a bit early. At first blush he seems to be a debonair, urbane oldster who runs a financial investment firm with a partner. Betty lives in the suburbs; Roy has a flat in London. They agree, given their age, that it’s hard to meet someone for the purpose of being simply good company. Soon, she discovers that Roy has a bad leg and struggles with the three flights of stairs to his apartment. Betty suggests that he use her guest room while his leg improves. This is against the advice of her grandson, Stephen (Russell Tovey) who is suspicious of Roy from the outset. Betty, however, is trusting and welcoming, though she makes it clear that their living arrangement is without benefits, so to speak. And it’s at this point that we begin to learn more about Roy, who still seems benign. They even take a trip to Berlin to tour and shop and reflect on WWII and their memories. The film title does frame the story and there are moments when you wonder if Betty is really the wealthy innocent, and Roy the shades of grey business guy who may see her as an invetment mark. She’s got a few million. But their rapport and connection seems consistently genuine. Until it isn’t. And that’s when act three betrays its enigmatic promise. Despite the best efforts of Mirren and McKellen, the film pretty much collapses. But watching them is witnessing a master class in acting and should be enjoyed for what it is: wonderful and a good enough reason to grab just under two hours and relish their individual gifts as they merge. The Good Liar. Directed by Bill Condon. Starring Helen Mirren, Ian McKellen and Russell Tovey. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The character “Astro Boy” was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books) and anime (movie and television animation), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries, and now Astro makes his debut in a feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh. Young moviegoers will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. This first installment (others will likely follow) explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy superhuman. He can fly, has machine guns in his butt, x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. Astro, at first unaware he’s a robot, sets out to find his place in the world, meaning, Metro City, an urban island hovering above earth which has been turned into a dumpsite for outdated robots and broken machinery. After being rejected by his father, who cannot accept that he’s a robot, Astro goes to earth and meets a group of kids, orphans from Metro City, all his own age. These discarded kids have no families. They are, however, human and Astro is reluctant to disclose that he is not. And so the story goes. The kids long for Astro’s powers and he longs for their humanity. He also grieves for the loss of his father. There’s an evil Mayor of Metro City (Donald Sutherland) who covets Astro’s “blue power,” a duplicitous hustler named Hamegg (Nathan Lane) who wants only to use Astro, and, finally, a long journey back into the arms of his dad. While the story brings to mind Transformers and Pinocchio (likely not known to young filmgoers), kids will find Astro appealing and will immediately look forward to The Return of Astro Boy. Astro Boy. Animated. With the voices of Nicolas Cage, Freddie Highmore, Nathan Lane, Kristen Bell and Bill Nighy. Directed by David Bowers. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Tales From Earthsea was adapted from the Ursula Le Guin Earthsea fantasy novels and directed by the son of the iconic Ghibli animator and storyteller, Hayao Miyazaki. For years he had pondered whether it would be possible to capture the breadth and depth of Le Guin’s extraordinary work in one animated film. Reluctantly he agreed to allow his son, Goro Miyazaki, who was not an experienced filmmaker, to bring Tales to the screen. The father’s instincts proved correct, and while the film was in production, he kept his distance. The result is considered by many to be Studio Ghibli’s only release that has been described as a “train wreck.” While the film has the extraordinary animation expected from the Studio, it’s the storytelling that puzzles. Some critics have referred to it as boring, pretentious, and not suited for younger audiences (late tweens and teens, possibly). Though the film does have a familiar feminist point of view, one known to thread its way through many of Ghibli’s animated stories, and does possess a spectrum of themes, such as the imbalance of nature, it remains jarring if not indecipherable. Ditto the characters. The narrative opens with medieval flying dragons engaging in battle, followed by the protagonist, Prince Arren (Jeff Bennett), inexplicably killing his father, the kindly king of the Earthsea kingdom. Taking his father’s Excalibur sword, he flees, later to be rescued by a wizard, also called Sparrowhawk (Timothy Dalton), who becomes Arren’s mentor. The wizard takes the Prince to a farmhouse where he meets Tenar (Mariska Hagitay), and Therru (Adi Teshima), her young daughter. Tenar saves his life when he falls ill, Arren and Sparrowhawk stay at the farm where they labor and the Prince matures. But the world is still not in balance. They discover that the cause of this disharmony is the evil Lord Cob (Willem Dafoe) who strives for immortality with the help of his henchman, Hare (Cheech Marin), a man who kidnaps and sells into slavery people from the countryside. There is a final confrontation between Lord Cob, Arren and Sparrowhawk, one that takes place at Cob’s abandoned castle. And thus concludes Arren’s quest, a dark journey of self-discovery, which is, in the main, overshadowed by harshly rendered villains. Tales From Earthsea (2006), Directed by Goro Miyazaki. A Studio Ghibli animé. With the voices of Jeff Bennett, Willem Dafoe, Timothy Dalton, Mariska Hargitay and Cheech Marin. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Goro Miyazaki’s Tales From Earthsea.

articles.text: California Revels returns to Oakland for its 35th season of one of the Bay Area’s premier holiday events. This year’s presentation is Unruly Magic: A Spirited Celebration of the Winter Solstice. Families, friends and holiday revelers are invited to watch wherever they may be, as this year’s production is entirely online, and can be viewed from December 12-20 at www.californiarevels.org. It will stream in High-Definition on Vimeo and YouTube, with live interactive components on Zoom. Audiences of all ages can celebrate the Winter Solstice with traditional music, dance, ritual, and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance.” The production features top musicians, actors, and featured performers. This year’s show includes Shay Black and Windborne Singers. Directed by Jeri Reed, newly filmed pieces are blended with archival footage to create a dynamic and moving feast for the eyes, ears, and spirit. The story of Unruly Magic Approaching the longest night of the year, a young Reveler turns to a magical staff to help her find a way through somber and troubled times. The staff, imbued Meara, from the 2019 Christmas Revels: A Solstice Journey Through Time. Meara is the main character of this year’s Christmas Revels: Unruly Magic. with ancient lore, takes her on an adventure that isn’t quite what she had in mind. Magic and mystery, spirits and song take the reins for this journey of the heart. The ancient traditions of bonfires, rituals, dances, and songs that have sustained generations through struggle and celebration are rekindled this Solstice, proving that tradition – and magic – live on. articles.text: For the scores of single 20 and 30 somethings of Piedmont, the nightlife scene has all but disappeared in the last few weeks due to the COVID- 19 induced curfew and stay at home order. Safety restrictions have been in place for almost nine months now, but it feels more like nine years. Staying up late and being out of the house, even if masked and alone, can give an illusion of a social life for us Millennials. (I prefer the label Gen Y). Beginning on November 21, California Governor Gavin Newsome enacted the curfew or “limited stay at-home order” that forbids non-essential work, movement and gathering between 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. When announced at the beginning of Thanksgiving week, the news decimated the collective of Piedmont’s hip, young, single crowd; goodbye Friendsgiving. Beginning December 7, outdoors and indoors dining is disallowed, hello Top Ramen. As of December 8, 54 of California’s 58 counties are in the purple tier, and 99.9 percent of the population. This status put the kibosh on Piedmont’s plan for the reopening of elementary schools at the start of December. Many parents may lament that today, December 9, is not the first week of school for their 5th graders. Within the ranks of Piedmont’s lively, unmarried population school may not be a concern but the curfew has grounded Piedmont’s night owls. Woe are we, Gen Y folk long for the days of hanging out front of Mulberry’s at 10:15 p.m. playing pickup sticks. It is just not as fun during the day. And whatever shall I do with all this nighttime bungee jumping gear I bought for the Oakland Ave. bridge? Should I bungee jump in the daytime in a glow in the dark suit? I think not. If you think the stock market stinks, the descent of the value of used bungee equipment will give you whiplash. I suppose no one trusts prestretched bungees or harnesses left out in the scorching Piedmont sun. With a curfew how can we head over the Piedmont border to pick up a late-night VHS at Silver Screen or a fancy new DVD at Video Room (still operating)? Did you know they disconnected the number for POPCORN (a machine that gave the precise time)? That number used to satiate the boredom of youth in the 90s. “At the tone, the time will be….too late to go out.” How about the paintball wars in Piedmont Park at night (with biodegradable paint of course), could a group activity be more socially distant? How can I howl at the moon from Scenic Ave. without leaving the house, a Zoom Howl? The portion of my stimulus check not used on bungee gear went into infrared night binoculars to document the behavior of nocturnal animals. How am I supposed to sleep with racoons, possums, skunks and owls skulking around unmonitored? They could be anywhere. Is nighttime street luging down Blair Ave. really a COVID risk? A curfew may be the best time to do so with fewer cars on the road. Oh well, it is all for the greater good, I suppose. After all, this virus stuff is no joke. Even the 20 and 30 somethings in Piedmont will have to sacrifice if we ever want to see an after-bedtime Roller Derby in Kiefer Court. One thing’s for sure, if vampires and werewolves were instrumental in spreading the virus, the curfew should help. Curbside pick up is always available. Just order and pick up! articles.text: Key volunteer with Turkey Trot, Center for the Arts, Chamber Music Festival Susan Freeman, a resident of Piedmont for 33 years, died on November 23, 2020 after battling cancer for five and a half years. She passed away surrounded by her loving family one week after her 70th birthday. Born on November 16, 1950 in Chicago, Illinois, she was the daughter of Peter and Rita Cotsirilos. She graduated from the University of Wisconsin, and received an MBA from Northwestern University in 1976, where she was one of few women to attend graduate business school. After college she took a job in the management training program at Harris Bank in Chicago, where she met her future husband, Peter. They were married in 1978 and moved to California that same year. Susan was a force of nature. Her energy filled the room and energized any task that she undertook. Susan was always quick to step in and offer help for new projects. She was a co-founder and leader for many years of the Piedmont Turkey Trot, which is now the city’s second largest public event. Her son Crosby was the overall winner several times, and he and his wife Jessica were the overall winners in 2019, the first couple to win the title. “Susan was instrumental in the revival and ultimate success of the Piedmont Turkey Trot,” said Marilyn Weber, current lead organizer. “Years ago, Susan called me when she learned that the leadership interest in managing and running the race was waning. She asked if we could work together to ensure that year’s race would happen. “This simple call started a many-year friendship. We both jumped in enthusiastically and developed a strong, collaborative and, most importantly, joyful friendship. Her ideas for improvements were never ending and her passion for this event and the community it served was endless,” she said. “What I will miss most about Susan was her deep care and affection for her family and friends. She was always there if you needed a good cheer or a good cry. She would be the friend you call if life’s obstacles were getting you down and she would always say, ‘Yes. What can I do to help?’” “We have lost a gem,” Weber added. Susan and her husband were active members of St. John’s Episcopal Church in Montclair, where she was an enthusiastic organizer of varied gala events. She was a key volunteer at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, where she was a mainstay of the annual weeklong Piedmont Chamber Music Festival. “Susan was a cherished presence and a tireless volunteer who ran our box office during the first few summers of the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival,” said co-founder Wayne Lee, a PiedLongtime resident and Piedmont volunteer Susan Freeman died on November 23 after battling cancer for nearly six years. She was 70. mont native. “She gave us her complete support, her cheeky and cheerful feedback and led by example when she took it upon herself to bring our uneaten refreshments to the homeless. We miss her dearly,” said Wayne Lee, co-founder of the annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival. “Susan Freeman not only handled the box office for theater productions at the Center for the Arts, she served as the unofficial den mother for the production team. She would see a need and without fanfare, would make things happen,’ said Sue Malick, president of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “Whether it was the Scottish National team lacrosse coach she brought from Scotland for the high school girls’ team, or college admission coaching for Piedmont students, or making sure that everyone had a seat for musical and theatrical productions at the Center, Susan made it work.” In her later years she was a college admissions coach and helped hundreds of high school students navigate through the challenge of college selection and applications. She sought the right fit and was justifiably proud that only two of her clients did not graduate from their original choices. Her children, Crosby and Libby, were products of the Piedmont schools from kindergarten through 12th grade. She was a talented cook who took great pleasure in hosting dinner parties. Through it all, Susan remained astoundingly hopeful and grateful for the life that had been given to her. She will be sorely missed. She is survived by Peter, her husband of 42 years, and by son Crosby and wife Jessica, and daughter Libby, all of Oakland. She is also survived by her mother Rita Cotsirilos, and siblings Steven, Patty, and Peter Jr. The family suggests that memorial donations in the name of Susan Freeman be made to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, c/o Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. Funds received will be used for a memorial tree which will be planted in the city in the future.

articles.text: As we finish up Thanksgiving leftovers and look forward to other food-centric holidays in December, food is on my mind. Turkeys, cookies, figgy pudding – food is an enduring part of the holiday season. Food is also an important issue in both the environmental and the humanitarian spheres. More than enough food is currently produced to feed everybody in the world, but 9 percent of the global population, or 670 million people, go hungry each year. A large amount is lost due to food waste, while a significant portion of grains go to biofuels and feeding livestock instead of people. There are numerous theories about how to feed the world, especially as our global population is projected to reach 10 billion by 2050. As we approach the goal of feeding everyone, we must also grapple with how to make food production less polluting. Environmentally, food is both an opportunity and a challenge. Our food system currently accounts for about 30 percent of global GHG emissions. This is larger than GHG emissions from either the transportation or energy sector. If we stopped all other emissions right now, emissions stemming from food would still stop us from meeting the goals outlined in the Paris Climate Accord. Meat, dairy, fish and eggs account for over half of food related emissions. Two-thirds of freshwater removal is for irrigation, while 43 percent of land is used for farming and livestock. As countries go through economic gains, more people want to eat red meat. This trend can be seen in places like China, where meat consumption has grown 15 times in the last 60 years. Raising enough livestock to feed more people is going to be difficult as we are simultaneously trying to reduce emissions. Fortunately, there are solutions. Relying on individual actions alone is unlikely to make a significant impact, but using policy to make change is one way to begin. The meat and dairy industries receive over $37 billion in federal subsidies annually. Using that money in other ways to encourage lower carbon diets could be a first step. Changing public health efforts to encourage less meat consumption could also make a difference. Meat isn’t the only issue. Changing how we farm can also make a big difference. Since the green revolution of the 1950’s, farmers have used fertilizers and mechanized systems to produce extraordinary yields. While the benefits of this style of farming seem obvious, there are drawbacks as well. Using fertilizers can lead to an insidious positive feedback loop, where more fertilizer needs to be used each year, requiring more resources annually. Relying on high yield practices can also mean more food waste. Examining farming techniques and consciously choosing lower carbon practices can both reduce emissions and costs, while keeping the farm land we all rely upon healthy for years to come. It is possible to both reduce emissions stemming from agriculture and feed everyone in a healthy way. The trick is determining how to do so, and quickly. Food is an important, and sometimes overlooked, aspect of climate change. Changing how individuals and countries eat food must be addressed now if we want to reduce emissions by a significant amount. In that vein, the City of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect are hosting a movie screening of Kiss That Ground on regenerative agriculture, which could be part of the solution we need. To sign up and take part in our free discussion visit this link: https://events. kissthegroundmovie.com/event/ piedmont-kiss-the-ground-community-discussion. Nate Redinbo is working in the Planning and Building Department for the next year as Piedmont’s Civic Spark fellow. He will be publishing a bi-monthly article on environmental topics that affect Piedmonters.

articles.text: The invention of farming changed human history forever. Before farming, humans were primarily hunter-gatherers. As we have adopted new methods of planting and procuring food, the world we rely on for resources has changed as well. It is time to come to a reckoning about the methods that we use to farm, eat food, and what resources we use along the way. Climate change has been influenced by many different sectors, but one that is not often talked about is agriculture. Following the “Green Revolution” of the 1960’s and the increased yields brought about by advancements such as increased pesticide usage and the mechanization of equipment, farming radically changed both domestically and internationally. While many of the outcomes have been beneficial, there have been serious side effects, including environmental outcomes that must be addressed immediately if we want our food production to continue. These issues and more are addressed in the documentary Kiss the Ground, which released this year. Although “soil health” doesn’t sound thrilling, I promise that the revelations from this documentary are surprising and worthwhile. Caring for our shared environment involves all of us, from policy makers to consumers to farmers. With all this in mind, the City of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect have teamed up to bring you a free screening of the documentary film, Kiss the Ground. Kiss the Ground is available on Netflix if you have an account, but you can also watch it for free on Vimeo through the city’s link. The screening became available to viewers on December 8 and will be available through Thursday, December 10. We are encouraging registration through the link. This free registration will let you watch the movie for free, join our Q & A session with Jessica Handy, a member of the film’s production team. Each two-person CATT team is comprised of a licensed clinician and a paramedic. They conduct evaluations of individuals possibly undergoing a mental health crisis and, if necessary, will transport the person to an appropriate facility or provide resources. A goal of the CATT project is “to provide better and more appropriate resources for people experiencing mental health crises or other issues when the police are frequently called to,” explained Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. ual when certain conditions are met. In the other four cases, CATT teams were unavailable due to demands on their time. The County pilot program began on July 20 with three teams and was expanded to five teams on October 11. articles.text: Funding signals go-ahead for playscape project at Linda-Beach The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) presented City Administrator Sara Lillevand with a check for $100,000 on December 2. The money will be used to help the Recreation Department move forward with its plans to redesign Linda-Beach Playfield, to include a playscape near the Oakland Avenue overpass. The check was presented to Lillevand by former PBF President Patty Siskind at the city’s virtual tree-lighting ceremony outside the Community Hall. The Linda Beach Master Plan conceptual design was adopted by City Council, and PBF helped make it a reality. In 2017, PBF began funding the design and installation of a new “playscape” at Linda Beach Playfield. The California Nature Playscape redesigns an area that is paved with asphalt into an outdoor recreation area for children. According to a brochure from the master plan, the all-new California Nature Playscape will “take full advantage of the topography of the site, connect to nature, and create climbing and play elements that allow for free-form exploration.” Once construction of the California Nature Playscape is completed, renovation of the Linda Beach tot lot will follow. The Tot Lot at Linda Beach is one of the most heavily used city recreation facilities and is long due for an upgrade. “$100,000 will go a long way to help us move forward with the Linda Beach master plan. The inspiration for the whole [project], was a wonderful community process, which several Piedmont Beautification Foundation members participated in,” Lillevand commented. “It will be an amazing addition to the city, and to an area between the Playfield and Oakland Avenue Bridge, which currently is not just underutilized, it’s unutilized.” Piedmont Beautification Foundation began working on the Linda Beach playscape project in 2017 following a master plan approved by council. Renderings are provided by PBF.
